changes.before: A heresy, in his book, is a teaching the church judged false.
changes.after: A heresy, to Epiphanius, was a wrong belief held by people led astray ever since Adam, the first man.
changes.source: HOLL1 13421-13423: "αἱρέσεών τε καὶ κακοδόξου γνώμης ἀνθρωπείας ὑπὸ πεπλανημένων ἀνδρῶν ... ἐξότε ἄνθρωπος ἐπὶ γῆς πέπλασται" (wrong belief spread by men led astray, "since man was formed on earth"). "Adam" names the first man formed.

changes.before: Later writers, from Augustine to a council at Nicaea four centuries on, took his book as their list.
changes.after: Later writers, from Augustine to a council at Nicaea four centuries after Epiphanius, took his book as their list.
changes.source: AUG 2414-2415 ("non modum, sed ordinem sum secutus"). MEN 26276-26281: the council treats the eighty chapters as a catalogue that "passes by none". MEN 26327-26331: "about four hundred years".

changes.before: The historian Sozomen, writing later, says he was born near Eleutheropolis and chosen bishop by the people of Cyprus.
changes.reason: Part 1, Rigor, "name a witness only where the listener would otherwise be misled"; no old source differs here.

changes.before: He wrote the Panarion about 375, by his own dating.
changes.after: He wrote the Panarion about 375.
changes.source: his own regnal date, HOLL1 13424-13426. The year is arithmetic on it (Holl's note 13447 only clarifies). The outline approves telling it plainly.

changes.before: Each chapter names a heresy, tells its teaching and answers it.
changes.after: Each chapter names a heresy, tells its teaching and answers it, twenty from before Christ's coming and sixty after.
changes.source: HOLL1 12512-12530 (the twentieth is the Herodians, then Christ's coming). Confirmed by AUG 2420-2424 ("separatis viginti ... sexaginta").

changes.before: He knew some heresies from books, some by hearsay, some with his own eyes and ears.
changes.after: He knew some heresies from books, some by report, some with his own eyes and ears.
changes.source: HOLL1 13429-13430: "τὰ μὲν ἐκ φιλομαθίας ἴσμεν, τὰ δὲ ἐξ ἀκοῆς ... ἰδίοις ὠσὶ καὶ ὀφθαλμοῖς". The Greek says "from study", and "books" is a fair plain word for it.

changes.before: He copied one opponent's own letter whole, so that no one could say he answered from hearsay alone.
changes.after: He copied one opponent's own letter whole, so that no one could say he answered from report alone.
changes.source: HOLL1 34006-34011 ("ἵνα μή τις νομίσειεν ἡμᾶς ἐξ ἀκοῆς μόνον"); the letter runs whole at 34016-34746.

changes.before: He listed even the followers of Apollinaris, a man he says was always dear to him.
In the 390s he preached against Origen in the church at Jerusalem.
changes.after: He preached against Origen in the church at Jerusalem.
changes.source: J6 40982-40983 "spoke against Origen in your church".

changes.before: The scholar Jerome, who was there and on his side, says the bishop of Jerusalem's party mocked him as an old fool.
Yet crowds pressed to kiss his feet.
changes.reason: Part 1, Rigor, fault 1: as its own sentence, the crowds' praise read as the narrator's, outside Jerome's credit.

changes.before: In a letter to that bishop Epiphanius says why.
changes.after: In a letter to the bishop of Jerusalem Epiphanius says why.
changes.source: Letter 51, to John (J6 10631-10632). It gives his charges against Origen (J6 10779-10782, 10813-10818).

changes.before: Origen, he writes, taught that souls were angels who fell into bodies, denied that this flesh would rise again, and read the garden of Eden as hidden meanings.
changes.after: Origen, he writes, taught that souls were angels who fell into bodies, denied that this flesh would rise from the dead, and read the garden of Eden as hidden meanings.
changes.source: J6 10813-10818 (souls once angels, cast down into bodies); J6 10899-10900 ("denies the resurrection of this flesh"); J6 10902-10903 ("explains allegorically all the trees"). Credited to him as a foe's charge.

changes.before: Genesis names the Euphrates among the rivers of paradise, and he writes: "I have also drunk from the great river Euphrates.
changes.after: Genesis, the first book of the Bible, names the Euphrates among the rivers of Eden, and he writes: "I have also drunk from the great river Euphrates.
changes.source: WEBBE line 271 ("The fourth river is the Euphrates"). The letter cites the four heads (J6 10914-10917).

changes.before: If the rivers were real, so was Eden.
changes.reason: the Do not say list, word for word; a narrator's summing-up of the quote.

changes.before: The same letter defends two acts of force.
Jerome's brother had fled the priesthood several times.

changes.after: In the same letter he defends what he did to the scholar Jerome's brother, who had several times run away from being made a priest.

changes.before: During a service near his monastery, he says, he had deacons seize the man and stop his mouth.
changes.after: During a service near Epiphanius's own monastery, he says, he had deacons, the clergy who serve under priests, seize the man and hold his mouth shut.
changes.source: J6 10686-10690 "the church of the villa which adjoins our monastery ... to seize him and to stop his mouth".

changes.after: The monks there had complained for a year that no one celebrated the sacraments, the church's holy rites, for them, he explains, and he feared they would drift from the church.
changes.source: J6 10704-10706 "For a year before I had heard many of them complain that they had no one to celebrate for them the sacraments"; J6 10657-10659 "alienating them from the Church with its ancient faith".

changes.before: He tore it apart and asked that such curtains be banned.
changes.after: Holding that an image of a man in church went against Scripture, he tore it apart and asked that such curtains be banned.

changes.before: Then Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, wrote to win him against Origen, though Theophilus had once accused Epiphanius of thinking God has a human form.
changes.after: Then Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, wrote to win him to his own campaign against Origen.
His letter said he had driven monks who followed Origen out of Egypt.
changes.source: Theophilus, Letter 90. J6 19716-19718: the church "has with the sword of the gospel cut down the Origenist serpents ... delivered ... the monks of Nitria". J6 19747-19748: "throughout all Egypt, because a few men have been expelled from the Church". J6 19729-19731: the three named men "have taken ship for Constantinople". It is a fair compression of the letter's force. Socrates confirms the expulsion (SS 17689-17693).

changes.before: The historian Socrates says Theophilus wanted revenge on monks he had driven out of Egypt, the Long Brothers, and used a man of simple mind and manners.
changes.after: The historian Socrates says Theophilus wanted revenge on those monks, the Long Brothers, and used Epiphanius, a man so devout that he was simple in mind and manners.
changes.source: SS 17886-17888 (Socrates 6.10): "Epiphanius being on account of his extraordinary piety a man of simple mind and manners was easily influenced by the letters of Theophilus".

changes.before: Sozomen says instead that Epiphanius had long loathed Origen's books, and that Theophilus saw no danger in following his example, because the people praised him.
changes.after: Another historian, Sozomen, says instead that Epiphanius had long loathed Origen's books, and that Theophilus saw no danger in following his example, because the people praised Epiphanius.

changes.before: There he ordained a deacon in the territory of its bishop, John Chrysostom, against church rules.
changes.after: There he made a man a deacon in the territory of its bishop, John Chrysostom, against church rules.
changes.source: SS 18083-18084; SS 18191-18193 "contrary to the ecclesiastical canon"; SS 18212-18213.

changes.before: He would not pray with John unless John condemned Origen's books and sent the Long Brothers away.
changes.after: He would not pray with John unless John condemned Origen's books and drove the Long Brothers from the city.

changes.before: Sozomen says one of those monks asked whether he had read any of their books.
changes.after: One of the Long Brothers asked him whether he had read any of their books.

changes.before: Augustine, who reports that Epiphanius set twenty heresies before Christ and sixty after, followed his order.
changes.after: Augustine wrote his own book on the heresies in the order of Epiphanius's list.

changes.before: Four centuries on, both sides in the quarrel over holy images claimed him.
changes.after: Four centuries on, when Christians quarreled over pictures of Christ and the saints in churches, both sides claimed him, and opponents of images quoted writings under his name.

changes.before: Opponents of images quoted writings under his name.
In 787 the council at Nicaea ruled that the passage was not his, arguing that his eighty chapters never listed the making of images.
changes.after: In 787 the council at Nicaea ruled that those writings were not his, arguing that his eighty chapters never listed the making of images.

changes.before: A reply written at Charlemagne's order answered with his own curtain letter.
changes.after: A book written to answer the council's argument replied with his own letter about the torn curtain.

changes.before: Epiphanius set one thing more after the eighty heresies in his chest of cures: the church, Christ's holy bride, which he says was there from the beginning.
changes.after: Epiphanius set one thing more after the eighty heresies in his chest of cures: the church, which he calls Christ's holy bride and says was there from the beginning.
changes.source: HOLL1 12395-12397 "μία δὲ μετὰ τὰς ὀγδοήκοντα ... Χριστοῦ νύμφη ἁγία ἐκκλησία, οὖσα μὲν ἀπ᾽ αἰῶνος".
